explanations.explanation: Two hundred fifty, baker! The text says these men of Israel were “…renowned as leaders of the congregation and representatives in the assembly.” (Numbers 16:2) These aren't strangers wandering in off the road. These are the folks with name tags that everybody recognizes. That's 250 big names joining one rebellion against Moses.

Seventy is a big crowd, friend, but this one is bigger. The text says 250 men of Israel joined, all renowned as leaders of the congregation and representatives in the assembly. That's a whole lot of important people leaning the same direction. Korah's side is a lot bigger than your guess.

Twelve could squeeze around one table, but this crowd needs a parking lot. The text says 250 men of Israel joined the rebellion. Every one of them was renowned as a leader of the congregation. That's a lot of important people all showing up for the same complaint.

explanations.answer: They're all holy and the LORD is in their midst
explanations.explanation: That's their whole argument. They say, “…everyone in the entire congregation is holy, and the LORD is in their midst.” Then they ask why Moses and Aaron, the priest, exalt themselves above the assembly of the LORD. They sound like they're making a point about the whole camp, but the target is Moses and Aaron.

explanations.answer: They're all weary and the LORD has heard their cry
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a sad song, friend, but it isn't what Korah's crew says. They say, “…everyone in the entire congregation is holy, and the LORD is in their midst.” Nothing about being weary here. This is a complaint aimed straight at Moses and Aaron.

explanations.answer: They're all ready and the LORD will raise new leaders
explanations.explanation: Close to a campaign speech, baker, but not what they say. The text has them saying, “…everyone in the entire congregation is holy, and the LORD is in their midst.” There's no promise of new leaders in their words. They just say Moses and Aaron have taken too much upon themselves.

Before Moses says one word back, he falls facedown. Most of us would be busy loading up a comeback, friend. The text doesn't tell us why he does it, and I'm not going to guess for it. It just says, "When Moses heard this, he fell facedown." (Numbers 16:4) His words to Korah and all his followers come after.

Tearing clothes is a big move, friend, but the text doesn't give it to Moses here. It says, “When Moses heard this, he fell facedown.” That's his first reaction, before he says a word. No fabric gets harmed in this verse.

That would be a fine plan, baker, but it's not what the text says. When Moses hears the charge, he falls facedown. Only after that does he speak to Korah and all his followers. The elders don't come up until later in the passage.

Censers is right. Moses tells Korah and his followers to take censers and put fire and incense in them in the presence of the LORD. A censer is what you carry that fire and incense in. The next day, the LORD will show whom He chooses.

Lamps would light up a room, friend, but Moses asks for something else. He tells Korah and his followers to take censers. Those are the ones that hold the fire and the incense. A lamp wouldn't be much help with the incense.

Jars are handy for plenty of things, baker, but not this test. Moses tells Korah and all his followers to take censers. Each one is to hold fire and incense in the presence of the LORD. I'd keep the jars on the shelf for this one.

True, baker. Korah's crew told Moses and Aaron, “You have taken too much upon yourselves!” Moses answers, “It is you sons of Levi who have taken too much upon yourselves!” He points their charge back at them and names exactly who he means. Clean return.

This one is true, friend. Korah's crew told Moses and Aaron they had taken too much upon themselves. Moses answers with “It is you sons of Levi who have taken too much upon yourselves!” That's their charge pointed back at them, with the sons of Levi named.

Moses says it plainly: “He has brought you near, you and all your fellow Levites, but you are seeking the priesthood as well.” The Levites already got the work at the LORD's tabernacle. Now they want the priesthood on top of it. Moses is asking if what they've been given isn't enough.

Offerings are not what Moses names, baker. He says, “…you are seeking the priesthood as well.” God had already brought the Levites near to do the work at the tabernacle. The extra thing they're after is the priesthood.

explanations.answer: Land of their own as well
explanations.explanation: Land never comes up in Moses' charge, friend. He says God brought the Levites near, “…but you are seeking the priesthood as well.” That's the extra thing he names. The Levites already have the tabernacle work, and now they want the priesthood too.

Close, but Moses puts it differently. He tells Korah, “Therefore, it is you and all your followers who have conspired against the LORD!” Then he asks about Aaron, “…who is he that you should grumble against him?” So the conspiring is against the LORD, and the grumbling is aimed at Aaron.

False is right, baker. Moses says, “Therefore, it is you and all your followers who have conspired against the LORD!” Then he asks about Aaron, “…who is he that you should grumble against him?” Two different words there: conspired against the LORD, grumbled against Aaron.

explanations.answer: A land flowing with milk and honey
explanations.explanation: You'd never guess it, but that's their word for Egypt. Dathan and Abiram, two Reubenites in Korah's rebellion, say, “…you have brought us up out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill us in the wilderness?” Then in the next verse they use that same phrase for the land they haven't reached yet. Milk and honey on both labels, baker.

explanations.answer: A land of chains and hard labor
explanations.explanation: That's the way you'd expect them to tell it, friend, but not what they say. Dathan and Abiram, two Reubenites, call Egypt “…a land flowing with milk and honey…” They say Moses brought them up out of it to kill them in the wilderness. That's quite the glow-up for a place they left.

explanations.answer: A land of dust and endless famine
explanations.explanation: No dust and famine here, friend. For Egypt, Dathan and Abiram, two Reubenites in the rebellion, say, “…a land flowing with milk and honey…” They add that Moses brought them out of it to kill them in the wilderness. Milk and honey is the phrase they pick, and I'd have asked to see the receipt.

That's the charge. Dathan and Abiram ask, “Must you also appoint yourself as ruler over us?” (Numbers 16:13) Watch that little word “also.” They've just said Moses brought them up to kill them in the wilderness, and now they pile this on top. It's like someone who hands you a full list of complaints and then says, "Oh, and another thing."

explanations.answer: Favoring his own tribe over theirs
explanations.explanation: Tribe favoritism isn't in their list, friend. Dathan and Abiram ask Moses, “Must you also appoint yourself as ruler over us?” That's the accusation they stack onto the first one. Their complaint is about Moses ruling over them.

explanations.answer: Hiding the LORD's words from them
explanations.explanation: That one never comes up, baker. What Dathan and Abiram say is, “Must you also appoint yourself as ruler over us?” They say it right after saying he brought them out to kill them in the wilderness. Nothing in their words is about hidden words from the LORD.

They say the opposite, friend. Dathan and Abiram tell Moses, “…you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey or given us an inheritance of fields and vineyards.” So no, they don't admit any fields and vineyards. They say they haven't received them.

False is right. Dathan and Abiram say to Moses, “…you have not brought us into a land flowing with milk and honey or given us an inheritance of fields and vineyards.” No admitting here. They're complaining that those things haven't happened.

A donkey is the answer. Moses tells the LORD, "I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them." (Numbers 16:15) The text says Moses is very angry when he says it, right after asking the LORD not to regard their offering. He's saying he hasn't taken even one from them. The text doesn't say why he names a donkey, so I'll just leave it right there.

An ox is a big animal to lose, friend, but Moses names a smaller one. He tells the LORD, “I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them.” It's a donkey in the text. Moses says he hasn't taken even one.

No coins in this verse, baker. Moses tells the LORD, “I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them.” The thing he names is a donkey, and he says not even one. Then he adds that he hasn't mistreated a single one of them.

Aaron isn't sitting this one out, friend. Moses tells Korah, “You and Aaron are to present your censers as well.” So it's 250 censers from the crowd, plus Korah's and Aaron's. Aaron stands in the test along with everyone else.

False is right. Moses says to Korah, “You and all your followers are to appear before the LORD tomorrow—you and they and Aaron.” Then he adds that Aaron is to present his censer as well. Aaron is in the test right alongside them.

That's what appears. When Korah has gathered his whole assembly against Moses and Aaron at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, “…the glory of the LORD appeared to the whole congregation.” It isn't just for the leaders. The whole congregation sees it.

A pillar of fire is a good guess for a camp like this, baker, but it isn't what the text says here. When Korah has gathered his whole assembly against Moses and Aaron, “…the glory of the LORD appeared to the whole congregation.” That's what everyone sees at the Tent of Meeting.

No angel is mentioned in this scene, friend. The text says that when Korah gathered his whole assembly against Moses and Aaron, “…the glory of the LORD appeared to the whole congregation.” That is what shows up at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.

That's not what happens, friend. The LORD says He will consume the congregation, and Moses and Aaron fall facedown. Then they ask Him, “…when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?” They don't step away quietly. They speak up for the people.

False is right. Moses and Aaron don't quietly step away. They fall facedown and say, “O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?” They speak up for the people.

Man is the word. Moses and Aaron ask, “O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?” They're lying facedown when they say it. I think that's a brave question to ask from the ground.

Tribe makes it sound bigger than it is, baker. Moses and Aaron say, “…when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?” The word in their question is man. They're asking if one man's sin should bring anger on everyone.
Family isn't the word they use, friend. Moses and Aaron ask God, “…when one man sins, will You be angry with the whole congregation?” They say it facedown. The sinner in their question is one man.
He doesn't go alone, friend. The text says, “So Moses got up and went to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel followed him.” The elders of Israel go with him. That's a walk with company.
False is right. Moses goes to Dathan and Abiram, and the elders of Israel follow him. He has company the whole way over. They're right there behind him.

Swept away is the warning. Moses tells the congregation, “Do not touch anything that belongs to them, or you will be swept away because of all their sins.” That's a serious reason to keep your hands to yourself. The people moved away from the dwellings of Korah, Dathan and Abiram.

explanations.answer: They'll be unclean for a week
explanations.explanation: A week of being unclean isn't the warning, baker. Moses says, “Do not touch anything that belongs to them, or you will be swept away because of all their sins.” That's far bigger than a week. Everybody backs away from their tents.

explanations.answer: They'll be sent outside the camp
explanations.explanation: Being sent outside the camp isn't the warning, friend. Moses says, “Do not touch anything that belongs to them, or you will be swept away because of all their sins.” He tells them to move away from the tents of these wicked men. They do.

explanations.answer: The earth opens and swallows them
explanations.explanation: That's what Moses says. He says, “…if the LORD brings about something unprecedented, and the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and all that belongs to them so that they go down alive into Sheol, then you will know that these men have treated the LORD with contempt.” This is a heavy part of the passage. It's the sign Moses names ahead of time.

explanations.answer: A flood sweeps their tents away
explanations.explanation: A flood would be quite a headline, friend, but Moses never mentions water. The sign he names is that "…the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and all that belongs to them…" (Numbers 16:30) The ground itself is what moves, not a river. I think this is a heavy part of the passage, and it's good to read it slowly.

explanations.answer: A storm tears their tents down
explanations.explanation: No storm in this one, baker. Nothing falls from the sky and no wind blows in Moses' words. He calls it something “unprecedented,” and then he spells it out: the earth opens its mouth, and they go down alive into Sheol. (Numbers 16:30) This is a heavy part of the passage.

True, and the timing is the point. The text says, “As soon as Moses had finished saying all this, the ground beneath them split open…” Nothing sits between his last word and the ground splitting. It's a heavy moment, baker.
This one is true, friend. The text says, “As soon as Moses had finished saying all this, the ground beneath them split open…” There's no gap between his words and what happens. It is a heavy moment.

Fled is the word. At their cries, all the people of Israel who were around them fled, saying, “The earth may swallow us too!” That's what they say as they run. I think fear drove them, baker, and this is a heavy moment.
Praying is a good instinct, baker, but the text says something else. At their cries, all the people of Israel who were around them fled. They said, “The earth may swallow us too!” They ran.

Weeping might fit that moment, friend, but the text has the people doing something else. At their cries, all the people of Israel who were around them fled. They said, “The earth may swallow us too!” It's a heavy moment, and they ran.

explanations.answer: Fire from the LORD consumes them
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The text says, “And fire came forth from the LORD and consumed the 250 men who were offering the incense.” They're the ones who stood there with their censers. It's a heavy ending to the test Moses set up.

explanations.answer: A plague from the LORD strikes them
explanations.explanation: A plague does come later in this passage, friend, but not here. For the 250 men offering the incense, “…fire came forth from the LORD and consumed…” them. The plague comes after the congregation grumbles the next day. This part is heavy.

explanations.answer: They're driven out of the camp
explanations.explanation: Nobody is driven out of the camp in this scene, baker. The text says, “And fire came forth from the LORD and consumed the 250 men who were offering the incense.” They're still holding the incense when it happens. This is one of the heavy parts.

explanations.answer: Hammer them into sheets for the altar
explanations.explanation: That's the instruction. The LORD says, “…hammer them into sheets to overlay the altar, for these were presented before the LORD, and so have become holy.” They will serve as a sign to the Israelites. So the censers end up on the altar.

explanations.answer: Bury them far outside the camp
explanations.explanation: Burying them is not what the LORD says, friend. He tells Moses to have the censers hammered “…into sheets to overlay the altar…” The reason He gives is that they were presented before the LORD and so have become holy. They're kept as a sign.

explanations.answer: Melt them into a bronze basin
explanations.explanation: A basin is a nice idea, baker, but it isn't the plan. The LORD says to hammer the censers into sheets to overlay the altar. They were presented before the LORD, so they have become holy. They will serve as a sign to the Israelites.

Aaron is the name. The reminder is “…that no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD, lest he become like Korah and his followers.” Korah's line runs back through Izhar, Kohath and Levi, and the reminder points to Aaron's descendants instead. The altar's new covering is there for everyone to see.

Moses is the one leading, friend, but the reminder names someone else. It says no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD. Eleazar, Aaron's son and a priest, took the bronze censers and had them hammered out to overlay the altar. So the name you're after is Aaron.

Levi is a close guess, baker, but Korah was a descendant of Levi and he still ended up in this story. The reminder says no outsider who is not a descendant of Aaron should approach to offer incense before the LORD. Being from Levi wasn't enough for the incense. The line that counts is Aaron's.

True, baker. The day after the ground swallowed Korah's men and fire took the 250, the people turn on Moses and Aaron with, “You have killed the LORD’s people!” (Numbers 16:41) After all that, the complaining is right back. I think this one is heavy, and it shows how quickly the grumbling can return.

That's actually true, friend. The text says the whole congregation grumbled against Moses and Aaron, saying, “You have killed the LORD’s people!” It happens the very next day. That's the charge they bring.

explanations.answer: Go to the congregation and make atonement
explanations.explanation: That's the job. Moses tells Aaron, “Take your censer, place fire from the altar in it, and add incense. Go quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them…” The censer is for the people out in the middle of the assembly. Aaron has a task to do and not much time.

explanations.answer: Offer it alone inside the Tent of Meeting
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't send him inside, friend. He says, “Go quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them…” So Aaron heads out to the people. The Tent isn't the destination.

explanations.answer: Carry it to the tents of Korah's families
explanations.explanation: Those tents aren't where Moses sends him, baker. He says, “Go quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them…” So the censer goes out to the people. Aaron runs into the midst of the assembly.
That's the reason. Moses says, “…wrath has come out from the LORD; the plague has begun.” So every moment matters. It's why he says to go quickly.

explanations.answer: The fire is spreading through camp
explanations.explanation: Fire isn't the trouble this time, friend. Moses says, “…wrath has come out from the LORD; the plague has begun.” The danger he names is the plague. That's why Aaron needs to go quickly.

explanations.answer: The cloud is about to lift
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the cloud lifting here, baker. Moses tells Aaron to go quickly because “…wrath has come out from the LORD; the plague has begun.” That's the urgency. Aaron has to move.

explanations.answer: Between the living and the dead
explanations.explanation: That's where he stands. The text says, “He stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted.” It's a heavy picture. Aaron stands right at the line.

explanations.answer: Beside the altar inside the Tent
explanations.explanation: Aaron isn't inside the Tent for this, friend. He runs into the midst of the assembly. Then the text says, “He stood between the living and the dead…” He's out where the people are.

explanations.answer: At the far edge of the camp
explanations.explanation: The edge of the camp is not where he ends up, baker. Aaron runs into the midst of the assembly with his censer. There he stands “…between the living and the dead…” He goes toward the trouble.

It's the other way around, friend. After Aaron offers the incense and makes atonement, the text says, “He stood between the living and the dead, and the plague was halted.” The plague stops. Aaron then returns to Moses at the Tent of Meeting.

False, friend. Aaron runs into the middle of the assembly, offers the incense and makes atonement for the people. Then the text says, “…the plague was halted.” It stops with Aaron standing between the living and the dead.

That's the number. The text says, “But those who died from the plague numbered 14,700, in addition to those who had died on account of Korah.” That's a heavy number. It tells you how serious the plague was.

Twenty-four thousand isn't the number here, friend. The text says, “But those who died from the plague numbered 14,700, in addition to those who had died on account of Korah.” That is a heavy part of the story. The number is 14,700.

Three thousand isn't the number in this passage, baker. The text says, “But those who died from the plague numbered 14,700, in addition to those who had died on account of Korah.” This is a heavy one. The number is 14,700.
